This is genuinely impressive. The six-agent architecture is a smart way to approach automated trading.

I built something along similar lines myself, starting with a crypto arbitrage scanner. But the interesting challenge wasn't finding trading opportunities.

It was making sure the system could explain, execute, and account for every decision.

So I took the concept further.

Grok Bot + GeckoTerminal + GoPlus Security + Python + SQLite.

Here's how I'd structure a more reliable six-agent trading system.

1. SCANNER — Find Opportunities

Use GeckoTerminal's API to discover new liquidity pools.

Collect token addresses, prices, liquidity, trading volume, and pool information.

Reject missing or invalid market data before analysis.

2. RUG CHECK — Investigate Token Risk

Connect GoPlus Security.

Check minting privileges, freeze authority, suspicious transfer controls, and available liquidity.

Unknown security information should block an entry, not be interpreted as safe.

No scanner can guarantee a token is rug-proof.

3. SIZER — Protect the Account

Calculate position sizes using actual available equity.

For an initial experimental configuration:

Maximum 10% equity per position.

Maximum two open positions.

Maximum 20% total exposure.

Stop-risk budget of 0.5% equity per position.

The engine checks these constraints before generating a simulated trade.

4. EXECUTOR — Model Real Trading Costs

Don't calculate profits using price differences alone.

Account for trading fees, slippage, estimated price impact, and transaction costs.

Start with paper execution.

Before enabling real transactions, a separate execution system would need validated quotes, independent risk controls, and transaction reconciliation.

5. LOGGER — Account for Every Decision

Store transactions and decisions in SQLite.

Record the entry price, quantity, costs, exit reason, and realized P&L.

Make the ledger independently reconcilable with the starting balance.

A dashboard displaying a profit isn't proof that the money was actually earned.

6. EQUITY ANALYST — Track Performance

Build a real-time dashboard showing:

Available cash.

Open positions.

Indicative portfolio equity.

Realized paper profit or loss.

Trade history and risk rejections.

THE COMPLETE ARCHITECTURE

Market Discovery
→ Token Security Screening
→ Position Sizing
→ Simulated Execution
→ Transaction Ledger
→ Equity Dashboard
→ Independent Verification
I turned this architecture into a runnable Python prototype with 15 passing automated tests.
It includes a browser dashboard, risk checks, simulated entries and exits, and transaction-ledger reconciliation.
The next challenge is validating execution against real exchange conditions.
That's where a promising trading experiment becomes a serious engineering project.
The real breakthrough isn't having six AI agents trading simultaneously.
It's building a system where every trade has a reason, every position has a risk limit, and every dollar can be accounted for.

note_tweet.text:
Grok Bot just built me a digital business card people can scan straight from my phone.

It uses Grok Bot Pages to create your card with your photo, name and contact details. 

It also generates a scannable QR code you can save on your phone to use whenever someone asks for your details.

Here’s the full prompt to create yours, complete with a public link and QR code. 

“Build me a digital business card as a Grok Bot Page, plus a QR code that opens it. Work step by step and check each step before moving on.

1 - Ask me for my details

Ask in one short message, all at once: full name, title, phone number, email, website, a photo of me and colour preference.

For the photo, ask for the original, high-resolution file, at least 1,500 pixels tall, ideally with a transparent background (a cut-out PNG). Chat apps often shrink photos, so ask for the original.

Default colours: dark navy with a blue accent.

Wait for my answers. Don’t invent anything. If something is missing, leave it off rather than using a placeholder.

2 - Prepare the photo

Check its resolution with a script. If it’s under about 1,000 pixels tall, tell me it may look blurry and ask for a bigger file before continuing.

If the background isn’t transparent, remove it or ask me for a cut-out.

Crop from just above the head to about the waist. Resize it to about twice the size it will display at, roughly 800 pixels tall, and save it as a WebP with transparency at quality 80, aiming for under 60,000 characters once base64-encoded.

Encode it to base64 with a script, never by hand. Record its length and MD5 checksum.

3 - Build the Page

Read the canvas skill first.

Make it look like a real physical business card: landscape, 85:55 ratio, rounded corners, soft shadow, centred on the page.

Size: maxWidth "min(900px, max(70vw, 600px), calc(80vh * 85 / 55))", width 100%, so it’s big on desktop and shrinks on a phone.

Left side: name in large bold white, title in a light accent colour, a short accent line, then phone, email and website, each with a Lucide icon (phone, mail, globe) in the accent colour. Phone uses tel:, email uses mailto:, website opens in a new tab.

Right side: the photo, standing on the card’s bottom edge and running off the right edge, with a faint glow behind it.

Background: a dark gradient in my colours. All text scales with the card’s width.

Keep every detail (name, title, phone, email, website, colours) in one list at the top of the code, so each is easy to edit later.

Embed the photo as a data URL inside the Page.

After saving, read the Page back and confirm the embedded photo matches the file’s length and MD5 exactly. If it doesn’t, fix it and check again.

4 - Publish

Give me the Page link, and tell me to turn on public link sharing from the Page’s share menu. Ask me to paste back the public link.

Remind me that anyone with the link can see it, so only include details I’m happy to share publicly.

5 - Create the QR code

Once I’ve sent the public link, use a Python script (qrcode or segno, plus Pillow) to make a 1,200 by 1,200 pixel QR code for it: error correction H, a white margin, dark modules in the card’s main colour.

Put the Grok Bot icon in the centre on a white rounded square, covering no more than 20% of the code’s width.

Also make a phone lock-screen version (1179 by 2556 pixels): card-colour background, the QR code centred on a white rounded panel, with ‘Scan for my card’ in bold white underneath.

Decode both images with a QR reader (zxing-cpp or pyzbar) and confirm they match the link character for character. Only then send them to me.

6 - Hand over

Send me the card link and both QR images.

Remind me to save the QR image to my phone’s favourites, or set the lock-screen version as my wallpaper, so people can scan my phone at events.

Then offer to change anything: colours, layout or details.”

@xai dropped 4 @bot  updates focused on SaaS waste, traffic visibility, and payment guardrails.

Here is the breakdown of what changed and how it impacts your spend:

1. Unused Subscription Detection and Price Tracking (v0.78.1)

What changed: Grok Bot added shopping cards and templates that find unused plans, watch price changes, and cancel tools after you confirm.

Why it helps the bill: Dead SaaS seats and quiet price hikes drain budgets every month. Catching and canceling idle plans stops recurring cash leaks fast.

What to do now: Run the new subscription templates against your active tool stack and cancel any seat with zero usage over the last 30 days.
Source: https://t.co/OhKzszhrmi

2. Route-Traffic Usage Visibility and Higher Routine Limits (v0.75.5)

What changed: You can now see route-traffic usage across connected workflows, store logins and cards in a Vault, and run routines with higher limits.

Why it helps the bill: Blind workflow traffic hides runaway API calls and wasted compute. Seeing exact route traffic lets you spot heavy steps before they spike your bill.

What to do now: Check route-traffic logs on your busiest automated routines and cap any path making extra calls.
Source: https://t.co/w6omebXKE4

3. Vault Payment Controls and CA Certificate Audit Logs (v0.77.0)

What changed: xAI added Vault payment controls, better plugin management, and enterprise audit logs for trusted CA certificate changes.

Why it helps the bill: Letting bots use saved cards without strict rules creates huge billing risk. Payment controls and audit logs stop rogue charges and track security changes.

What to do now: Turn on Vault payment controls before adding company cards and route CA audit logs to your security team.
Source: https://t.co/jIDs42uutP

4. Smarter Auto-Review and Scheduling Logic (v0.75.8)
What changed: Grok Bot improved auto-review rules, task scheduling, and Slack plugin handling to cut down on manual approval steps.
Why it helps the bill: Bad scheduling causes duplicate runs, and constant manual approvals waste engineer hours. Better logic cuts both compute waste and team wait time.
What to do now: Update your Slack and connector workflows to use the new auto-review rules for low-risk tasks.
Source: https://t.co/dermK5qb9e
